cards.text: Baker, these are the words of a man named Amos, and what he saw concerns Israel. It came two years before the earthquake, when Uzziah was king of Judah and Jeroboam son of Jehoash was king of Israel. So who is this guy?

cards.question: Amos is about to carry the LORD's words. Amos was among the ___ of Tekoa.

cards.text: A sheepherder from Tekoa, and I'm a cookie stamper who did years in a junk drawer, so who am I to judge a résumé? Then Amos says the LORD roars from Zion, and friend, that is not a whisper, that is a ROAR.

cards.question: True or false: when the LORD roars from Zion, the pastures of the shepherds rejoice.

cards.text: Then the LORD speaks, and He starts with Damascus, the head of Aram (Isaiah 7:8). He says, "For three transgressions of Damascus, even four, I will not revoke My judgment," and He's got more to say.

cards.question: The LORD says He will not revoke His judgment on Damascus. What does that mean?

cards.text: And the LORD says why: Damascus threshed Gilead with sledges of iron. Friend, I'm a cookie stamper, and I know a heavy press when I hear one.

cards.question: The LORD names the house of Hazael and Ben-hadad, kings of Aram (2 Kings 13:3, 24). He says He will send ___ upon the house of Hazael to consume the citadels of Ben-hadad.

cards.text: Then He gets specific: He will break down the gates of Damascus and cut off the rulers in the Valley of Aven and Beth-eden. I once gave a baker directions by pointing my mustache and saying "over there," and friend, the LORD does not do "over there."

cards.question: True or false: the LORD says that after He breaks down the gates of Damascus, the people of Aram will get to stay in their land.

cards.text: Next up is Gaza, a Philistine city (Joshua 13:3), and there's that line again: three transgressions, even four, and no taking back the judgment. Hear it twice and you know it like the beep of your own oven timer.

cards.question: The LORD says Gaza exiled a whole population, delivering them up to Edom. What happened to those people?

answers.text: They were handed over to another nation
They were sent home in peace
They were hidden from their enemies

cards.text: So the LORD will send fire upon the walls of Gaza. Then He names Ashdod, Ashkelon and Ekron, like a whole group chat getting called out one name at a time.

cards.question: True or false: after Ashdod, Ashkelon and Ekron, the LORD says whoever is left of the Philistines will be spared.

cards.text: Next is Tyre, a fortified city (Joshua 19:29), and Tyre also delivered up a whole congregation of exiles to Edom. On top of that, the LORD says Tyre broke a covenant of brotherhood.

cards.question: The LORD says Tyre broke a covenant of brotherhood. What does that mean Tyre did?

answers.text: It broke a bond made like brothers
It broke a deal to pay its debts
It broke a pact to guard the sea

cards.question: Tyre's sentence matches Gaza's. What does the LORD say He will send upon the walls of Tyre?

cards.text: That fire will consume Tyre's citadels too. Three nations in, and nobody's walked away clean.

Next on the list is Edom, and Esau, Jacob's twin brother, is the father of the Edomites (Genesis 25:24-26; 36:9). And there's that line again, three transgressions, even four, so by now you could say it right along with Him.

cards.question: Edom's charge sounds personal. What does the LORD say Edom did?

answers.text: Pursued his brother with the sword

cards.question: True or false: the LORD says Edom's anger flared up once and then cooled off.

cards.text: So the LORD will send fire upon Teman to consume the citadels of Bozrah. Teman, Bozrah, friend, I need a map just to keep up, and I live on a planet barely big enough for my bakery.
Then come the Ammonites, descended from Lot, Abraham's nephew (Genesis 12:5; 19:36, 38). What they did is hard to even say out loud: they ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead.

cards.question: The Ammonites ripped open the pregnant women of Gilead. What does the LORD say they did it for?

cards.text: So the LORD will kindle a fire in the walls of Rabbah, the Ammonite city (2 Samuel 12:26). It comes with war cries on the day of battle and a violent wind on the day of tempest.

cards.question: The LORD says the Ammonite king will go into ___, he and his princes together.

cards.text: Next the LORD turns to Moab, also descended from Lot (Genesis 19:36-37). This time, what Moab did wasn't to Israel or Judah, it was to the king of Edom.

cards.question: Moab's transgression was against Edom's king, not against Israel or Judah. True or false: the LORD still judges Moab for it.
What does the LORD say Moab did to the king of Edom?

answers.text: Took his crown as a prize

cards.text: So the LORD will send fire against Moab, on the citadels of Kerioth. He says Moab will die in tumult, with war cries and the sound of the ram's horn.

cards.question: True or false: the LORD says only the ruler of Moab will be cut off, and his officials will be spared.

cards.text: And now the list comes home: the next name is Judah, where Amos's own town of Tekoa sits (2 Chronicles 11:5-6). It's like nodding along in a meeting while everybody else gets called out, and then the boss says YOUR name.

cards.question: The LORD's charge against Judah is that they reject the ___ of the LORD and fail to keep His statutes.

cards.text: Did you catch that, friend? Every nation before was judged for what it did to people, but Judah's charge is about what it did with the Law of the LORD.

cards.question: Judah is led astray by the lies their fathers walked in. What does that say about Judah's problem?

cards.text: So Judah gets the same sentence as the nations: fire upon Judah to consume the citadels of Jerusalem. And friend, Amos isn't done talking yet.

findings.problem: The joke compares Damascus threshing Gilead with iron sledges, an atrocity against people, to Papa Dorin's own cookie stamping ('I know a heavy press when I hear one'). This makes light of the victims' suffering instead of treating their situation with respect. The image is also muddled: he knows a press 'when I hear one.'

rule.text: Humor about people in Bible stories looks at their human situation with respect.

findings.problem: The question already says Gaza 'exiled a whole population, delivering them up to Edom,' so it gives away the right answer, 'They were handed over to another nation.' Given that setup, the wrong answers 'They were sent home in peace' and 'They were hidden from their enemies' are ruled out and read as silly.

rule.text: A setup line can't rule out the wrong answers either.

findings.problem: The right answer, 'It broke a bond made like brothers,' is the only one that echoes 'covenant of brotherhood,' so it stands out from 'debts' and 'guard the sea.' It also adds 'like,' which the text does not have, and so narrows a phrase the text leaves open.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike.

findings.problem: The 'I will send fire upon...' sentence repeats in every oracle. The baker already answered 'fire' on stop 1 card 8, and card 13 told the same sentence for Gaza. Asking it again for Tyre is a repeated line, and 'Tyre's sentence matches Gaza's' gives the answer away.

rule.text: When a line repeats, like a psalm's refrain, ask about it only the first time it appears.

findings.problem: 'This time, what Moab did wasn't to Israel or Judah' implies that the earlier nations' victims were Israel or Judah. The text never says who Gaza and Tyre exiled or who Edom's 'brother' is, and the walkthrough never says Gilead belongs to Israel. The card connects things the text leaves open.

rule.text: Leave open what the text leaves open: who is being spoken to, why, or how two things connect.

findings.problem: The right answer 'Law' is capitalized while 'prophets' and 'temple' are lowercase. The capital letter flags the right answer.

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike.

findings.problem: The right answer and 'It started this year' are both about when Judah's problem began. 'It came from Edom' is about where it came from, which is a different kind of answer.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The passage's story group is 'none,' but the last story card ends with a story-isn't-over line: 'And friend, Amos isn't done talking yet.' That line only belongs on a passage in a story group that isn't the last passage in it. (The oracle series does continue at Amos 2:6, so if it should carry on, the grouping needs fixing in the Passages step.)

rule.text: If the passage is in a story group and isn't the last passage in it, the last story card ends with a short line from Papa Dorin saying the story isn't over (or the teaching isn't done).

findings.problem: Most story cards in stop 2 are plain retellings with no voice, for example cards 7, 9, 12 and 16. Only cards 4 and 14 have a real laugh. Some moments rightly stay serious, like the Ammonites on card 5. But Moab and the Judah turn could carry real humor or more energy without muddying a fact.

rule.text: When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
